source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Thomas Paine (writing as “the author of Common Sense”)

source.excerpt: THESE are the times that try men’s souls. The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.
trail: The complete essay opens with the line and continues “The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot …” — confirmed in the full primary text.
The pamphlet was first published on 19 December 1776 in Philadelphia, per Wikipedia’s account of The American Crisis.
A 1776 Boston broadside printing survives in the Library of Congress, attributed to “the author of Common Sense.”

author.heading: About Thomas Paine
author.metaLine: 1737–1809 · English-born American revolutionary, author of Common Sense
author.bio: Thomas Paine (1737–1809) was an English-born political writer whose pamphlets helped galvanize the American Revolution. His Common Sense (January 1776) made the case for independence, and The American Crisis series that followed sustained morale through the war’s darkest months. He later wrote Rights of Man and The Age of Reason.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Paine wrote the first Crisis essay in December 1776, when Washington’s army was in retreat and the Revolution looked close to collapse. The pamphlet was meant to steel a demoralized public and a dwindling army.
According to tradition, Washington had it read aloud to his troops before they recrossed the Delaware to strike at Trenton on 26 December 1776.
